title: The street that said no to cars
subtitle: When one city street closed to traffic for a summer, the people who lived there found out more about each other than they expected.
text: Every morning for eleven years, Marta Silva watched the same queue of cars crawl past her front window on Calder Street. The road was a short cut between two busier ones, and drivers used it all day long. {1} So when the city council asked residents whether they would like to close the street to traffic for a summer, she was the first to sign the form.

Not everyone was so enthusiastic. Some neighbours worried about deliveries, others about where they would park, and one elderly man wrote a long letter to the local paper predicting that the street would be taken over by strangers. {2} In the end, the council agreed to a trial: twelve weeks, with large wooden planters at each end of the street and access only for emergency vehicles. Residents who needed a car would have to park on the next road and walk the last hundred metres home.

The first few days were strange. People stood on the empty road as if they were not sure they were allowed to be there. {3} By the end of the first week, however, a group of children had chalked a football pitch onto the tarmac, and someone had carried a table outside and left it in the middle of the road, where it stayed for the rest of the summer.

That table turned out to be important. It belonged to the Okafor family, who had lived at number 14 for six years without, as Mrs Okafor admits, knowing anyone's name. {4} Soon the table was being used for card games in the evenings, and a second and a third table had appeared beside it.

Not all the changes were so welcome. The street became noticeably louder after dark, and two residents complained that they could no longer sleep with their windows open. {5} A rota was drawn up, and quiet hours were agreed for weeknights after ten o'clock. Volunteers took turns to remind people, politely, when it was time to move indoors, and the complaints soon stopped.

When the twelve weeks were over, the council carried out a survey. Traffic on the surrounding roads had increased only slightly, and there had been no accidents at all on Calder Street. {6} Of the 64 households, 58 voted to keep the planters exactly where they were. Several families who had been planning to move away said they had changed their minds.

Even the man who wrote to the newspaper has changed his mind. He now runs a small library from a bookcase outside his front door. 'I was wrong about the strangers,' he says. 'The problem was that we were strangers to each other.'
sentences: Rather than give up the experiment, the neighbours decided to sort the problem out themselves.
Most of them had never been inside each other's houses.
It was noisy, it was dangerous for children, and nobody who lived there actually needed it.
More surprising was the result of the vote among the residents themselves.
Even the cats seemed suspicious, keeping close to the walls.
Meetings were held, petitions were signed, and the arguments went on for most of the spring.
On the first Saturday, she put a pot of coffee on it and invited anyone who passed to help themselves.
why: 'It' is the road just described; 'So when…' follows from her reasons to dislike it.
The arguments of the spring end with 'In the end, the council agreed…'.
'Even the cats' adds to the people who were unsure; 'however' then turns to the change.
'She' is Mrs Okafor and 'it' is the table; the coffee explains why 'soon the table was being used'.
'The problem' is the noise just described; 'A rota was drawn up' is how they sorted it out.
'More surprising' follows the survey figures and introduces 'Of the 64 households…'.
